doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Television, vocal albums and orchestral craft
title: Five- and six-way saxophone voicings and drop twos
summary: Mandel explains his preference for five- and six-way saxophone voicings, using at least two altos, and compares his usage with Thad Jones's drop-two voicings.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: There is one, I don’t know how much in detail you remember those charts but I was just listening to “A Foggy Day,” the other night and there’s a sax section background you write behind Sinatra's vocal that sounds to my ears it sounds like a five way voicing with a drop two. Do you remember? It's an unfair question to ask any writer what he did with specific voicing on a specific record but I can't help but ask.

I generally favor five way voicing’s, I’m not really one of those four-part harmony with a double-lead writers. I don’t do that a lot, unless I want that particular effect, but that's not I’d say a general working tool for me. I like writing five ways very much, I like writing six ways, I love having six saxophones better than anything else but I found out if I make my records with six saxophones they sound wonderful on the record but the minute the singer wants to go out on the road with them, I have to re-voice them for five and that’s a pain in the you- know-what.
Absolutely.

I have to totally re-voice them then, and it's double work plus it just doesn't sound as good for five, so you know I'm sort of pushed into going with five but I sort of feel like five way writing has all been pretty well exploited to its maximum. I’d like having six or seven saxophones even because there’s all kinds of ways to use them, that I can think of.
Yeah, the five way voicing I was talking about on “Foggy Day,” reminded me… like the end of the 60s Thad Jones started using a lot of soprano lead.
Yep.
And I mean the voicing’s you wrote for Sinatra were pretty high which is the reason I thought they were dropped twos.
Dropped twos? What are dropped twos, that’s what I was starting to wonder?
When you take the second highest voice and drop it an octave, if you have a close voicing.
Oh, I know what you’re talking about, you mean when you got six way… I know what you mean.
When you have a close voicing.
You drop, yeah, you take the second highest and drop it…
An octave.
So that you got – it’s almost like… yeah I know what you’re talking about. So you have a space between the first and third voice.
Exactly.
Sometimes I’ll do that.
That was one of Thad Jones’ favorite saxophone voicings.
I do that quite often, yeah.
Only…
Whereas if you have six or seven brass you can just plain do it without leaving anything out.
Um-hm.
So you can do it with six or seven saxophones too.
Exactly. I think it works particularly well say when the lead alto line is pretty high on the horn.
Pretty high on the horn yeah.
So, I mean it was interesting for me to hear that segment just because it was something Thad did a few years later with soprano lead, but you were doing it earlier with the alto lead.
Um-hm, it’s another reason why I like at least two altos, I don’t like having that top tenor up there too much, I mean it's okay up there but it's a different sound.
And it's hard for a lot of players to play in tune up there consistently.
I’d say so, and also the one alto sticks out. There's not something to blend it with, in fact if I have six saxophones, I’ll use three altos, three, two, and one is a wonderful sound.
